opus-5.5.text:
I think the brain is actually a very useful reference point, not because we need to copy it neuron by neuron, but because it shows us what the problem really is.

If you think about what the brain does, it's constantly taking in a huge stream of sensory input: light hitting your retina, sound, touch, your body's own sense of where it is. That raw signal is incredibly high-dimensional and noisy. But you don't experience the world as pixels. You experience objects, space, other people, causes and effects. So the first thing the brain does is build an internal representation, a compressed and structured picture of what's out there. To me that's the core of a world model: it's not the input itself, it's the abstraction you build from the input.

The second part is that this representation isn't passive. The brain is always predicting. When you reach for a cup, your brain already has an expectation of how heavy it is, what it'll feel like, where your hand will be a few hundred milliseconds from now. When the prediction is wrong, if the cup is empty when you thought it was full, you notice immediately. That loop, predicting what happens next, especially as a consequence of your own actions, and correcting when you're wrong, is what I'd call the essence of a world model.

And then the third part is behavior. The reason you have this internal model at all is so you can act. You can simulate in your head: if I do this, what happens? You can plan, you can imagine, you can avoid touching the hot stove without having to actually burn yourself first. So the pipeline is something like perception into representation, representation into prediction and simulation, and simulation into decision and action.

What I find interesting is how this contrasts with where a lot of AI has been. Large language models are amazing, but they mostly live in the space of language, which is already a highly processed, human-made abstraction of the world. Language is kind of the output of a world model, not the world model itself. A child learns an enormous amount about physics, objects, and intuitive causality before they can say a single sentence. Animals that have no language at all clearly have rich world models. A cat jumping onto a table is doing a lot of sophisticated prediction.

So when I think about building world models in AI, I think the key questions are: can we learn good representations directly from sensory data, especially vision, which is the richest channel we have? Can those representations support prediction, not necessarily at the level of every pixel, but at the level of what matters? And can that be connected to action, so the system can actually use its model to reason and plan?

I also want to be a bit careful. People sometimes equate world models with video generation, being able to generate a realistic-looking next frame. That's related, but I don't think it's the same thing. The brain doesn't render a photorealistic movie of the future. It predicts at an abstract level, the things that are relevant for what you want to do. Generating pretty pixels might be one way to train the representation, but the real goal is understanding, not rendering.

So in one sentence: a world model, in the brain's sense, is an internal, predictive, action-oriented representation of the world, learned largely from sensory experience. And I think getting that right, especially grounding it in vision, is one of the most important open problems on the path to more general intelligence.

r001.rationale: It describes sensory input as a huge, high-dimensional stream, but does not contrast its bandwidth with the lower bandwidth of human communicative output.

r002.rationale: It describes a world model as an internal representation built from sensory input that supports prediction, simulation, decisions, and action.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the brain is actually the best reference point we have, because it's the only working example of a general world model that we know of. If you look at how the brain handles sensory input, the first thing you notice is that it doesn't try to reconstruct the world pixel by pixel. The retina is receiving something like ten million bits per second, and only a tiny fraction of that ever becomes conscious or drives action. The brain is aggressively compressing, and it's compressing toward what matters for behavior, not toward what's needed to reproduce the image.

That's a very important point for how we think about world models in AI. A lot of the early work, including things I've been involved in on the vision side, was framed around reconstruction: can you predict the next frame, can you regenerate the input. But the brain tells you that's probably not the objective. The objective is to build an internal representation that supports prediction, planning, and action, and reconstruction is at best a proxy. Sometimes it's a misleading proxy, because you spend capacity modeling things like the texture of a wall or the noise in a video that have nothing to do with what you need to do next.

The second thing I take from neuroscience is the idea of prediction as the core computation. There's this predictive coding view where the cortex is constantly generating expectations about incoming signals, and what gets passed forward is mostly the error, the surprise. So perception is not passive. The brain is running a model of the world all the time and checking it against the senses. That's really what a world model is: a system that has an internal state, uses it to anticipate what comes next, and updates when it's wrong. In that sense, the "world model" isn't a separate module that you bolt onto a perception system. Perception itself is already model-based.

The third piece, and I think this is where we are furthest behind, is the loop with behavior. In the brain, perception, memory, and motor control are not cleanly separated stages. The representation you build is shaped by the actions you can take. A child learns what a cup is partly by grasping it, dropping it, seeing it roll. So the representation is grounded in affordances, in what you can do with the thing. Most of our current vision models are trained on static images or videos scraped from the internet, with no agency at all. They've seen the world but never acted in it. I think that's why they can be very good at describing a scene and still fail at simple physical or spatial reasoning. They never had to close the loop.

So when I try to understand a world model through the brain, I come back to three principles. Compress toward what's useful for behavior, not toward reconstruction. Make prediction the central operation, so perception and modeling are the same thing. And ground the whole system in action, so that the model is learned by interacting with the world rather than just watching it. If you build something that does those three things, I'd be comfortable calling it a world model, even if it looks nothing like a video generator.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts high-rate retinal input with the small fraction that reaches consciousness or drives action, but it does not compare sensory bandwidth with communicative output.

r002.rationale: It describes a predictive internal model updated against sensory input and discusses grounding representations in action, but does not clearly identify the world model as transforming sensory input into behavioral output.

astra-6.text:
I think a useful way to understand a world model is to start with the gap between sensing and acting. You receive visual information, sounds, touch, but those signals don’t directly tell you what to do. You need some internal understanding of what’s happening around you and how your actions might change it.

Imagine reaching for a cup. You have some expectation of where it is, how heavy it might be, and what will happen when you touch it. You don’t consciously solve all of that physics. You act based on your expectations, receive feedback, and adjust. If the cup is much lighter than you expected, that mismatch helps update your understanding.

So, to me, a world model is an internal model that supports that loop: perception, prediction, action, and feedback. It doesn’t necessarily need to reconstruct every detail of the environment. It needs to capture the things that matter for anticipating what happens next, especially when you intervene.

Of course, that’s a useful analogy, rather than a claim that we know exactly how the brain implements it. But it gives us an important question for AI: can a system use what it perceives to predict the consequences of its actions and adapt when those predictions are wrong?

r001.rationale: The response discusses sensory input and action but does not contrast the bandwidth of sensory input with the lower bandwidth of communication.

r002.rationale: It describes an internal model that connects perception to prediction, action, and feedback, conveying a model that turns sensory input into behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a useful way to understand a world model is to ask what sits between perception and action. We receive sensory input—images, sounds, touch—but we don’t simply map each input to a fixed response. We build some internal understanding of what’s happening around us, and that understanding helps us decide what to do next.

For example, if you reach for a cup, you have expectations about where it is, how heavy it might be, and what will happen when you touch it. You don’t have to consciously calculate all of that. But your behavior depends on those predictions, and when something unexpected happens, you update your understanding.

So, to me, a world model isn’t necessarily a system that reconstructs every detail of the world. It’s an internal representation that captures enough of the world’s structure and dynamics to support prediction and action. And the interesting question for AI is: what do we need to learn from sensory experience so that we can do that reliably? I think the brain gives us a useful motivation, although we should be careful not to assume we already understand exactly how it accomplishes this.

r001.rationale: The response discusses sensory input and behavior but does not compare the bandwidth of sensory input with communicative output.

r002.rationale: It describes a world model as an internal representation between perception and action that uses sensory-based predictions to guide behavior, and connects this idea to the brain.
